items.stem: Which term describes a company that owns or controls production in more than one country and organises its activities on a global scale?
items.answer: Transnational corporation (TNC)
items.markingKey: Transnational corporation (TNC): a company that owns or controls production in more than one country and organises its activities on a global scale. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “global commodity chain”, and give one example.
items.answer: The network of labour and production processes that brings a product from raw materials to the consumer. Example: cocoa grown in West Africa becoming chocolate sold in Europe.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the network of labour and production processes that brings a product from raw materials to the consumer); 1 mark for a relevant example such as cocoa grown in West Africa becoming chocolate sold in Europe. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “outsourcing” and “race to the bottom”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Outsourcing: contracting out part of the production process to other companies, often in lower-wage countries (e.g. a phone company using a separate supplier to assemble handsets). Race to the bottom: competition between countries to attract TNCs by lowering wages, taxes and regulations (e.g. governments weakening labour laws to keep factories).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: An electronics TNC opens an assembly plant in an export processing zone near Madrid, employing 8,000 young women on short contracts. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: TNCs exploit cheap labour and resources in poorer countries; profits flow to owners in the core, and governments compete in a race to the bottom (Sklair, Klein).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A mining company owned by shareholders abroad extracts copper near Lagos; the government receives low royalties, and local rivers become polluted. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: TNCs exploit cheap labour and resources in poorer countries; profits flow to owners in the core, and governments compete in a race to the bottom (Sklair, Klein).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using structured interviews to research the size and growth of TNC investment in different countries.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present. Limitations: they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the size and growth of TNC investment in different countries but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a company that owns or controls production in more than one country and organises its activities on a global scale?
items.answer: Transnational corporation (TNC)
items.markingKey: Transnational corporation (TNC): a company that owns or controls production in more than one country and organises its activities on a global scale. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “transfer pricing”.
items.answer: The pricing of goods traded between branches of the same TNC, which can be used to shift profits to low-tax countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the pricing of goods traded between branches of the same TNC, which can be used to shift profits to low-tax countries. [1]

items.stem: Priya, a sociology student, is designing a project on the size and growth of TNC investment in different countries. Explain one strength of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the size and growth of TNC investment in different countries. [2]

items.stem: A mining company owned by shareholders abroad extracts copper near Bogotá; the government receives low royalties, and local rivers become polluted. Explain how neoliberal and transformationalist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neoliberalism: TNCs bring investment, jobs, technology and access to global markets; governments should remove barriers so that growth trickles down. Transformationalism: TNCs are powerful global actors, but states can still bargain with and regulate them; effects vary between countries.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: The table shows official data on investment by TNCs in three developing countries. Table: inflows of foreign direct investment by TNCs (billion dollars) | 2005 | 2020. Country A | 11 | 22. Country B | 20 | 35. Country C | 8 | 10. (a) Calculate the change, in billion dollars, for Country C between 2005 and 2020. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that TNC investment brings development to poorer countries.
items.answer: (a) 10 − 8 = +2 billion dollars. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Country A, Country B, Country C; Country B had the highest figure for 2020. Some countries became less attractive as wages rose or instability grew. Qualifications: Investment figures do not show who benefits; profits may be repatriated; jobs may be low-paid; investment may leave quickly. The data also come from official statistics of 3 countries in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 8 and 10; 1 mark for +2 billion dollars (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes lacking the minimum resources needed for physical survival, such as food, water and shelter?
items.answer: Absolute poverty
items.markingKey: Absolute poverty: lacking the minimum resources needed for physical survival, such as food, water and shelter. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “absolute poverty”? Give one example.
items.answer: Lacking the minimum resources needed for physical survival, such as food, water and shelter. Example: living on less than about $2 a day.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (lacking the minimum resources needed for physical survival, such as food, water and shelter); 1 mark for a relevant example such as living on less than about $2 a day. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “official development assistance (aid)” and “debt crisis”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Official development assistance (aid): grants and cheap loans from governments of richer countries to poorer countries (e.g. a donor government funding a vaccination programme). Debt crisis: a situation in which poorer countries cannot repay loans and spend large shares of income on interest (e.g. a government spending more on debt repayments than on health).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A donor government gives a large grant to build a dam near Colombo, on condition that the work is done by companies from the donor country. Suggest how a dependency sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Dependency theory: aid and debt keep poorer countries dependent; tied aid and loan conditions serve donor interests and transfer wealth to the core (Hayter, Frank).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A donor government gives a large grant to build a dam near Mumbai, on condition that the work is done by companies from the donor country. Explain how a neoliberal sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neoliberalism: aid distorts markets and supports inefficient governments; growth comes from free trade, private investment and reducing state spending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: An international charity funds clean-water pumps in villages around Lagos, run and repaired by local committees. Explain how neoliberal and modernisation sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neoliberalism: aid distorts markets and supports inefficient governments; growth comes from free trade, private investment and reducing state spending. Modernisation theory: aid fills the investment gap and provides technology and expertise so that poorer countries can reach take-off (Rostow, Sachs).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Ana, a sociology student, is designing a project on changes in levels of global poverty. Evaluate the use of official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they cover very large numbers of people, often a whole population, so they are representative. Limitations: interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public; they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in levels of global poverty but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Hana, a sociology student, is designing a project on changes in levels of global poverty. Evaluate the use of longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; they show how people’s lives change over time and allow cause and effect to be explored. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in levels of global poverty but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes lacking the resources needed for the normal standard of living of the society one lives in?
items.answer: Relative poverty
items.markingKey: Relative poverty: lacking the resources needed for the normal standard of living of the society one lives in. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “official development assistance (aid)”?
items.answer: Grants and cheap loans from governments of richer countries to poorer countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: grants and cheap loans from governments of richer countries to poorer countries. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “absolute poverty” and “relative poverty”?
items.answer: Absolute poverty: lacking the minimum resources needed for physical survival, such as food, water and shelter. Relative poverty: lacking the resources needed for the normal standard of living of the society one lives in.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: The table shows World Bank estimates of the share of people in extreme poverty. Table: percentage of the population living in extreme poverty | 1990 | 2019. Sub-Saharan Africa | 50% | 30%. South Asia | 45% | 8%. East Asia and Pacific | 60% | 1%. By how many percentage points did the figure for South Asia change between 1990 and 2019?
items.answer: -37 percentage points
items.markingKey: 8 − 45 = -37 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: The table shows World Bank estimates of the share of people in extreme poverty. Table: percentage of the population living in extreme poverty | 1990 | 2019. Sub-Saharan Africa | 52% | 38%. South Asia | 47% | 9%. East Asia and Pacific | 61% | 6%. (a) Calculate the gap between East Asia and Pacific and South Asia in 1990 and in 2019, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that global poverty is being successfully reduced.
items.answer: (a) 1990: 14 percentage points; 2019: 3 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure fell for Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, East Asia and Pacific; Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest figure for 2019. Rapid industrial growth in East Asia (especially China) lifted many out of poverty. Qualifications: Population growth means numbers in poverty may fall less than percentages; the poverty line is very low; relative inequality between rich and poor countries has grown. The data also come from official statistics of 3 people in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (14 and 3); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: The table shows World Bank estimates of the share of people in extreme poverty. Table: percentage of the population living in extreme poverty | 1990 | 2019. Sub-Saharan Africa | 54% | 40%. South Asia | 48% | 15%. East Asia and Pacific | 57% | 1%. (a) Calculate the gap between South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa in 1990 and in 2019, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of extreme poverty. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that global poverty is being successfully reduced.
items.answer: (a) 1990: 6 percentage points; 2019: 25 percentage points; the gap widened. (b) They are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure fell for Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, East Asia and Pacific; Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest figure for 2019. Debt, conflict and dependence on primary exports slowed progress in parts of Africa. Qualifications: Population growth means numbers in poverty may fall less than percentages; the poverty line is very low; relative inequality between rich and poor countries has grown. The data also come from official statistics of 3 people in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (6 and 25); 1 mark for “widened”. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes an international organisation that lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems and promotes financial stability?
items.answer: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
items.markingKey: International Monetary Fund (IMF): an international organisation that lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems and promotes financial stability. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “International Monetary Fund (IMF)”, and give one example.
items.answer: An international organisation that lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems and promotes financial stability. Example: emergency loans to a country in a currency crisis.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (an international organisation that lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems and promotes financial stability); 1 mark for a relevant example such as emergency loans to a country in a currency crisis. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “conditionality” and “trade liberalisation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Conditionality: the requirement that a borrower adopts certain policies in return for a loan (e.g. cutting subsidies as a loan condition). Trade liberalisation: the removal of tariffs, quotas and other barriers to trade (e.g. reducing import taxes on foreign rice).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: After a currency crisis, the government near Auckland accepts an IMF loan on condition that it cuts fuel subsidies and sells the state electricity company. Suggest how a dependency sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Dependency theory: these organisations are dominated by core countries and impose policies that keep the periphery dependent and open to exploitation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Farmers near Muscat lose their incomes after the country removes import tariffs under a trade agreement, and cheap subsidised grain floods in from abroad. Explain how a neoliberal sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neoliberalism: the IMF, World Bank and WTO promote free markets, privatisation and fiscal discipline, which create the conditions for growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Ana, a sociology student, is designing a project on how farmers experience trade liberalisation. Evaluate the use of non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts; the researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively. Limitations: observation schedules impose the researcher’s categories on behaviour; the researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it. Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how farmers experience trade liberalisation but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “World Trade Organization (WTO)”.
items.answer: An international organisation that sets and enforces rules for trade between member countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: an international organisation that sets and enforces rules for trade between member countries. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “World Trade Organization (WTO)” and “Washington Consensus”.
items.answer: World Trade Organization (WTO): an international organisation that sets and enforces rules for trade between member countries. Washington Consensus: the set of neoliberal policies (privatisation, deregulation, free trade, spending cuts) promoted by the IMF and World Bank.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the effects of loan conditions on public services. Explain one strength of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the effects of loan conditions on public services. [2]

items.stem: After a currency crisis, the government near Mumbai accepts an IMF loan on condition that it cuts fuel subsidies and sells the state electricity company. Explain how transformationalist and neoliberal sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Transformationalism: they are part of an emerging system of global governance that reshapes, but does not remove, state power; reform is possible (Held, Stiglitz). Neoliberalism: the IMF, World Bank and WTO promote free markets, privatisation and fiscal discipline, which create the conditions for growth.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the network of labour and production processes that brings a product from raw materials to the consumer?
items.answer: Global commodity chain
items.markingKey: Global commodity chain: the network of labour and production processes that brings a product from raw materials to the consumer. [1]

items.stem: State one reason why TNCs locate production in developing countries.
items.answer: Weaker regulation of labour and the environment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. weaker regulation of labour and the environment. [1]

items.stem: Explain Sklair’s argument that a transnational capitalist class of TNC executives, officials and professionals promotes global capitalism and consumerism, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Sklair argued TNCs drive the culture-ideology of consumerism and are the main agents of global capitalism. Criticism: Others argue states still regulate TNCs and that TNCs bring jobs and technology.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Official statistics show foreign direct investment (FDI) by TNCs in three countries. Table: inflows of foreign direct investment by TNCs (billion dollars) | 2005 | 2020. Country A | 11 | 37. Country B | 29 | 44. Country C | 7 | 9. By how many billion dollars did the figure for Country A change between 2005 and 2020?
items.answer: +26 billion dollars
items.markingKey: 37 − 11 = +26 billion dollars. [1]

items.stem: Freya, a sociology student, is designing a project on the size and growth of TNC investment in different countries. Explain two limitations of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. The interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. 2. The interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the size and growth of TNC investment in different countries. [4]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why TNCs are powerful in the global economy.
items.answer: Size of revenues; mobility (footloose); control of global commodity chains; lobbying governments; control of technology and brands; transfer pricing and tax avoidance.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Size of revenues; mobility (footloose); control of global commodity chains; lobbying governments; control of technology and brands; transfer pricing and tax avoidance. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes grants and cheap loans from governments of richer countries to poorer countries?
items.answer: Official development assistance (aid)
items.markingKey: Official development assistance (aid): grants and cheap loans from governments of richer countries to poorer countries. [1]

items.stem: State one criticism made of international aid.
items.answer: Loans create debt.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. loans create debt. [1]

items.stem: Sachs argued that extreme poverty can be ended through large increases in well-targeted aid. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Sachs argued poor countries are stuck in a “poverty trap” and need a “big push” of aid for health, education and infrastructure. Criticism: Easterly argues aid often fails because it is planned from above.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Modernisation theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Karachi wants to research changes in levels of global poverty. Explain one strength of using self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of changes in levels of global poverty. [2]

items.stem: International estimates of extreme poverty in three world regions are shown below. Table: percentage of the population living in extreme poverty | 1990 | 2019. Sub-Saharan Africa | 51% | 34%. South Asia | 51% | 19%. East Asia and Pacific | 59% | 1%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Sub-Saharan Africa change between 1990 and 2019?
items.answer: -17 percentage points

items.stem: The table shows World Bank estimates of the share of people in extreme poverty. Table: percentage of the population living in extreme poverty | 1990 | 2019. Sub-Saharan Africa | 54% | 38%. South Asia | 49% | 18%. East Asia and Pacific | 55% | 1%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for South Asia between 1990 and 2019. Show your working. (b) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) (18 − 49) ÷ 49 × 100 = -63.3%. (b) The figure fell for Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, East Asia and Pacific; Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest figure for 2019.

items.stem: Explain two arguments for and against aid.
items.answer: For: funds health, education and infrastructure; emergency relief; fills investment gap (Sachs). Against: tied aid; debt; corruption; dependency (Hayter); undermines local markets (Moyo).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: For: funds health, education and infrastructure; emergency relief; fills investment gap (Sachs). Against: tied aid; debt; corruption; dependency (Hayter); undermines local markets (Moyo). [8]

items.stem: (a) Explain two arguments for and against aid. (b) Assess the claim that aid does more harm than good to developing countries.
items.answer: (a) For: funds health, education and infrastructure; emergency relief; fills investment gap (Sachs). Against: tied aid; debt; corruption; dependency (Hayter); undermines local markets (Moyo). (b) For: Dependency and neoliberal critics: tied aid, debt, conditions, corruption, dependency, undermining local producers (Hayter, Moyo, Easterly). Against: Aid has reduced child mortality and disease (Sachs); targeted and multilateral aid can work; NGOs and participatory projects; the problem is design not aid itself. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on how far the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: For: funds health, education and infrastructure; emergency relief; fills investment gap (Sachs). Against: tied aid; debt; corruption; dependency (Hayter); undermines local markets (Moyo). [8] (b) Level 1 (1-3): a few simple points. Level 2 (4-6): some explained arguments, mainly on one side; limited evaluation. Level 3 (7-9): a range of explained arguments and evidence for and against, with some evaluation. Level 4 (10-12): a balanced, well-supported analysis using theories, studies and concepts, sustained evaluation and a reasoned conclusion. For: Dependency and neoliberal critics: tied aid, debt, conditions, corruption, dependency, undermining local producers (Hayter, Moyo, Easterly). Against: Aid has reduced child mortality and disease (Sachs); targeted and multilateral aid can work; NGOs and participatory projects; the problem is design not aid itself. [12]

items.stem: Outline what Sachs meant by arguing that well-designed international action and aid can help end extreme poverty.
items.answer: Sachs criticised harsh IMF austerity but supported international organisations funding health and infrastructure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Sachs criticised harsh IMF austerity but supported international organisations funding health and infrastructure. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “trade liberalisation” and “Washington Consensus”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Trade liberalisation: the removal of tariffs, quotas and other barriers to trade (e.g. reducing import taxes on foreign rice). Washington Consensus: the set of neoliberal policies (privatisation, deregulation, free trade, spending cuts) promoted by the IMF and World Bank (e.g. conditions requiring privatisation of water supply).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Lina, a sociology student, is designing a project on the effects of loan conditions on public services. Explain two strengths of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: 1. Regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified. 2. They cover very large numbers of people, often a whole population, so they are representative.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the effects of loan conditions on public services. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying the effects of loan conditions on public services.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of loan conditions on public services but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.answer: The network of labour and production processes that brings a product from raw materials to the consumer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the network of labour and production processes that brings a product from raw materials to the consumer. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which TNCs may benefit developing countries.
items.answer: Create jobs and pay wages higher than local alternatives; bring investment, technology and skills; build infrastructure; pay taxes; connect local suppliers to global markets.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: The table shows official data on investment by TNCs in three developing countries. Table: inflows of foreign direct investment by TNCs (billion dollars) | 2005 | 2020. Country A | 11 | 21. Country B | 21 | 35. Country C | 7 | 13. By how many billion dollars did the figure for Country C change between 2005 and 2020?
items.answer: +6 billion dollars
items.markingKey: 13 − 7 = +6 billion dollars. [1]

items.stem: A global sportswear brand closes its factory in Manila and moves production to a country where wages are half as high, after the local government raised the minimum wage. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: TNCs exploit cheap labour and resources in poorer countries; profits flow to owners in the core, and governments compete in a race to the bottom (Sklair, Klein).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics for studying the size and growth of TNC investment in different countries.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; positivists see them as objective “social facts” that can be used to test hypotheses. Limitations: they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them; interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the size and growth of TNC investment in different countries but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes aid given on condition that the recipient buys goods or services from the donor country?
items.answer: Tied aid
items.markingKey: Tied aid: aid given on condition that the recipient buys goods or services from the donor country. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “debt crisis”?
items.answer: A situation in which poorer countries cannot repay loans and spend large shares of income on interest.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a situation in which poorer countries cannot repay loans and spend large shares of income on interest. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between absolute and relative poverty, using an example of each.
items.answer: Absolute: lack of minimum needed for survival (e.g. insufficient food); relative: lacking what is normal in one’s society (e.g. cannot afford school trips).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark each example. [4]

items.stem: An international charity funds clean-water pumps in villages around Toronto, run and repaired by local committees. Suggest how a dependency sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Dependency theory: aid and debt keep poorer countries dependent; tied aid and loan conditions serve donor interests and transfer wealth to the core (Hayter, Frank).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: International estimates of extreme poverty in three world regions are shown below. Table: percentage of the population living in extreme poverty | 1990 | 2019. Sub-Saharan Africa | 50% | 38%. South Asia | 45% | 11%. East Asia and Pacific | 57% | 4%. By how many percentage points did the figure for South Asia change between 1990 and 2019?
items.answer: -34 percentage points
items.markingKey: 11 − 45 = -34 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: International estimates of extreme poverty in three world regions are shown below. Table: percentage of the population living in extreme poverty | 1990 | 2019. Sub-Saharan Africa | 58% | 39%. South Asia | 50% | 15%. East Asia and Pacific | 59% | 1%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Sub-Saharan Africa between 1990 and 2019. Show your working. (b) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) (39 − 58) ÷ 58 × 100 = -32.8%. (b) The figure fell for Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, East Asia and Pacific; Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest figure for 2019.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (39 − 58) ÷ 58 × 100; 1 mark for -32.8% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark for each accurate pattern supported by figures from the table. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using laboratory experiments to research the experiences of villagers affected by an aid project.
items.answer: Strengths: results are quantitative and easy to compare; the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability. Limitations: it is impossible to control all the variables that affect human behaviour; participants who know they are being studied may change their behaviour (the Hawthorne effect or demand characteristics). Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of villagers affected by an aid project but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: (a) Explain two arguments for and against aid. (b) To what extent do sociological arguments and evidence support the view that aid does more harm than good to developing countries?
items.answer: (a) For: funds health, education and infrastructure; emergency relief; fills investment gap (Sachs). Against: tied aid; debt; corruption; dependency (Hayter); undermines local markets (Moyo). (b) For: Dependency and neoliberal critics: tied aid, debt, conditions, corruption, dependency, undermining local producers (Hayter, Moyo, Easterly). Against: Aid has reduced child mortality and disease (Sachs); targeted and multilateral aid can work; NGOs and participatory projects; the problem is design not aid itself. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on how far the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: For: funds health, education and infrastructure; emergency relief; fills investment gap (Sachs). Against: tied aid; debt; corruption; dependency (Hayter); undermines local markets (Moyo). [8] (b) Level 1 (1-3): a few simple points. Level 2 (4-6): some explained arguments, mainly on one side; limited evaluation. Level 3 (7-9): a range of explained arguments and evidence for and against, with some evaluation. Level 4 (10-12): a balanced, well-supported analysis using theories, studies and concepts, sustained evaluation and a reasoned conclusion. For: Dependency and neoliberal critics: tied aid, debt, conditions, corruption, dependency, undermining local producers (Hayter, Moyo, Easterly). Against: Aid has reduced child mortality and disease (Sachs); targeted and multilateral aid can work; NGOs and participatory projects; the problem is design not aid itself. [12]

items.stem: Which term describes an international organisation that lends to developing countries for development projects and reforms?
items.answer: World Bank
items.markingKey: World Bank: an international organisation that lends to developing countries for development projects and reforms. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Voting power in the IMF is equal for all member countries.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Votes are weighted by financial contribution, giving rich countries most power.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Sachs argued that well-designed international action and aid can help end extreme poverty. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Sachs criticised harsh IMF austerity but supported international organisations funding health and infrastructure. Criticism: Easterly argues top-down plans by international bodies often fail.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Modernisation theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: The table shows the share of government spending in a country before and after an IMF programme. Table: share of government spending (%) | Before the programme | After the programme. Health | 12% | 9%. Education | 15% | 11%. Debt repayment | 16% | 25%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Health change between Before the programme and After the programme?
items.answer: -3 percentage points
items.markingKey: 9 − 12 = -3 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: After a currency crisis, the government near Kuala Lumpur accepts an IMF loan on condition that it cuts fuel subsidies and sells the state electricity company. Explain how a dependency sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Dependency theory: these organisations are dominated by core countries and impose policies that keep the periphery dependent and open to exploitation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying the effects of loan conditions on public services.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of loan conditions on public services but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]
